limitations: Current wayfinding research lacks a model that can include both human and environmental factors and determine their relative importance in the complex process. (page 25)
Space syntax underplays the significance of metrics such as distance and direction. (page 23)
Space syntax overlooks the relevance of the overall shape and layout of the environment, as well as the importance of the shape and pattern of path layouts. (page 23)
Space syntax ignores superficial aspects of an environment such as surface colours, patterns, and textures. (page 23)
Cognitively based computation models are based heavily on human aspects of wayfinding and lack environmental aspects. (page 24)
minimum_safe_summary: This narrative review synthesizes existing research on wayfinding, defining it as the process of navigating to a destination using environmental cues. It highlights the complexity of wayfinding, which involves an interplay of human factors (e.g., spatial ability, gender, culture, biological factors) and environmental factors (e.g., layout, landmarks, signs, maps, color, light). The paper discusses various cognitive and mathematical models used to understand and quantify wayfinding ease, such as the Visibility Index (VI), Inter-connection Density (ICD), and Space Syntax. Key findings indicate that clear signage, salient landmarks, and specific color/lighting choices can improve wayfinding performance, while increased layout complexity (higher ICD) can hinder it. A significant limitation identified is the lack of a holistic model that integrates both human and environmental factors to determine their relative importance in wayfinding.
